vignette:
Samir is a thirty-four-year-old publisher who came to therapy at his wife’s urging, though he would not have said he needed it. The traumatic event that reshaped his life happened eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon. His younger brother, Tariq, was stabbed to death on a city bus during a botched robbery. Samir had been at home, just out of the shower, his skin still damp, when his mother called screaming. He can still hear the pitch of her voice, the word “Tariq” repeated like a siren. He remembers grabbing a towel, leaving wet footprints across the hardwood, the phone slipping from his hand. That moment—naked, dripping, utterly unprepared—has become the emotional center of his vulnerability. He cannot be undressed in a room where he might receive bad news. He showers only when his wife is home and he knows the phone is off. Even then, he leaves the bathroom door open, listening.

The bus itself is now unthinkable. Samir used to take the 47 downtown to his office. Now he drives, even when traffic doubles his commute, because the moment he sees a bus his chest locks and his attention narrows to the faces around him. He has become a compulsive reader of expressions. On the subway platform, in the grocery store, at his daughters’ school pickup, he scans for anyone who looks agitated, restless, or too still. He notices potential weapons everywhere: a man’s bulky jacket pocket, a car’s tire iron in plain view, a set of keys held like a blade. When he is tired—and he is almost always tired now, because he sleeps poorly and wakes often—this scanning becomes exhausting but he cannot stop it. Fatigue makes him feel exposed, as though his guard has dropped, and that feeling alone is enough to send him home early from work or cancel plans.

His memories of that afternoon do not form a coherent story. He can see fragments: the phone screen, the towel on the floor, the hallway stretched too long. The most intrusive piece is auditory—his mother’s voice, but also a sound he did not hear himself, something the police told him about: a bystander’s scream recorded on the bus security footage. Samir has never seen the footage, but he hears that scream in his head, over and over, like a film reel stuck on one frame. The replay is worst at night, when he is lying still, or when he is too exhausted to fight it.

The consequences have been concrete. Samir has stopped attending work events that are held in unfamiliar neighborhoods. His publishing firm recently launched a book at a venue across town, a place he had never been, and he told his boss he was sick. He has lost touch with two colleagues who used to meet him for coffee near the bus stop; he stopped suggesting alternatives, and eventually they stopped asking. His wife has taken over all school pickups and grocery shopping because Samir cannot walk into a store without cataloging exits and sharp objects. He knows this is not sustainable. He has come to therapy because last week, when his daughter asked him to take her to a new park, he said no without explaining why, and she cried. He sat in the car afterward, studying his own face in the rearview mirror, trying to see if he looked dangerous. That was the moment he agreed to call for help. He is afraid of what he might become if this continues—a man who cannot be naked in his own home, who reads every stranger’s face as a threat, who cannot take his daughter to a park. But more than that, he is afraid that no amount of vigilance will ever keep anyone safe again.
